overview.title: Contents (continued): chapters 14-16
overview.main_topic: Contents entries for section 14.5 (sequence models), chapter 15 (language models and the Transformer) and chapter 16 (text generation).
overview.central_idea: The book goes from word embeddings and recurrent text models to language modeling, sequence-to-sequence learning and the Transformer, then to training a mini-GPT, using pretrained LLMs (Gemma, instruction tuning, LoRA) and current LLM techniques (RLHF, multimodality, RAG, reasoning models).
overview.importance: This is the map of the book's coverage of modern NLP and large language models.
learning_objectives: Locate word embeddings and their pretraining in 14.5.
Find dot-product attention, the Transformer encoder/decoder blocks and positional embeddings in 15.3.
Locate the mini-GPT, sampling strategies, LoRA, RLHF and RAG material in chapter 16.

paragraphs.excerpt: Training a recurrent model 406 ■ Understanding word embeddings 409 ■ Using
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 14.5 'Sequence models' lists training a recurrent model (406), understanding word embeddings (409), using a word embedding (410), pretraining a word embedding (414), and using the pretrained embedding for classification (418).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Order-aware text models are introduced together with dense word vectors, including pretraining them and reusing them.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Embeddings are the input representation for all later language models.

terminology.meaning: a learned dense vector representing a token, where geometric relations reflect meaning

paragraphs.excerpt: English-to-Spanish translation 430 ■ Sequence-to-sequence learning with RNNs 432
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 15.2 'Sequence-to-sequence learning' lists English-to-Spanish translation (430) and sequence-to-sequence learning with RNNs (432).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Translation is the running seq2seq task, first solved with RNNs before the Transformer.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Seeing the RNN version first motivates what attention improves.

terminology.meaning: mapping an input sequence to an output sequence, e.g. translation

paragraphs.excerpt: Dot-product attention 439 ■ Transformer encoder block 444 Transformer decoder block 446
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 15.3 'The Transformer architecture' lists dot-product attention (439), the Transformer encoder block (444), decoder block (446), sequence-to-sequence learning with a Transformer (448), and embedding positional information (451).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The Transformer is built up piece by piece: attention, then encoder and decoder blocks, then a full translation model, then positional information.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the architecture behind modern LLMs, including the mini-GPT of chapter 16.

terminology.meaning: weighting values by the softmax of query-key dot products
information added to token embeddings to encode their position

paragraphs.excerpt: Pretraining a Transformer encoder 454 ■ Loading a pretrained Transformer 455 ■
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 15.4 'Classification with a pretrained Transformer' lists pretraining a Transformer encoder (454), loading a pretrained Transformer (455), preprocessing IMDb movie reviews (458) and fine-tuning (460).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The IMDb task from chapters 4 and 14 is revisited with a pretrained Transformer encoder.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Comparing the same task across chapters shows how much pretraining contributes.

terminology.meaning: training on a large generic task before adapting to a specific one

connections: p.130: the IMDb dataset in chapter 4 (printed 106)

paragraphs.excerpt: What makes the Transformer effective? 461 16 Text generation 466 16.1 A
paragraphs.what_it_says: This merged element lists 15.5 'What makes the Transformer effective?' (461), the chapter 16 title 'Text generation' (466), 16.1 'A brief history of sequence generation' (468) and 16.2 'Training a mini-GPT' (470).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Chapter 15 ends with an analysis of the Transformer; chapter 16 begins with history and then a small GPT-style model.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Building a mini-GPT makes the mechanics of LLMs concrete.

terminology.meaning: a decoder-only Transformer trained to predict the next token

connections: p.485: what makes the Transformer effective (printed 461)

paragraphs.excerpt: Building the model 473 ■ Pretraining the model 476 Generative decoding 478
paragraphs.what_it_says: Under 16.2 the subsections are building the model (473), pretraining the model (476), generative decoding (478) and sampling strategies (480).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Generation needs both a trained model and a decoding procedure that chooses the next tokens.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Sampling strategy strongly affects output quality and diversity.

terminology.meaning: the rule for choosing the next token from the model's predicted distribution

paragraphs.excerpt: Text generation with the Gemma model 485 ■ Instruction fine-tuning 488 ■
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 16.3 'Using a pretrained LLM' lists text generation with the Gemma model (485), instruction fine-tuning (488) and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) (490).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The book moves to a real pretrained LLM and shows how to adapt it to follow instructions efficiently.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: LoRA makes fine-tuning large models feasible on modest hardware.

terminology.meaning: training an LLM on instruction-response examples
fine-tuning by learning small low-rank updates to weight matrices

paragraphs.excerpt: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) 495 Multimodal LLMs 498 ■ Retrieval
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 16.4 'Going further with LLMs' lists RLHF (495), multimodal LLMs (498), retrieval augmented generation (RAG) (501) and 'reasoning' models (502).
paragraphs.what_it_means: A survey of techniques that extend basic LLMs: alignment with human feedback, other modalities, retrieval, and reasoning.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: These connect directly to how current AI assistants are built; the scare quotes around 'Reasoning' anticipate the book's critical view in chapter 19.

terminology.meaning: retrieving relevant documents and supplying them to the LLM as context

connections: p.588: chapter 19, the future of AI (printed 564)

deeper.title: Using printed vs. PDF page numbers
deeper.body: The numbers in this table of contents are the book's printed page numbers. This companion links by PDF page number. For the main body of the book, **PDF page = printed page + 24** (for example, chapter 15 starts on printed page 421, which is PDF p.445; chapter 16 on printed 466, PDF p.490). The offset was checked against the chapter-opener pages; it is a property of this PDF, not something the book states.

misconceptions.claim: The page numbers in the contents are the PDF page numbers.
misconceptions.correction: They are printed page numbers. In this PDF the main body is offset by 24 pages (e.g. printed 16 = PDF p.40).

later.note: Chapter 15 opener: language models and the Transformer.

takeaways: Word embeddings (14.5) are the bridge from bag-of-words to Transformers.
Chapter 15 builds the Transformer from dot-product attention up, then fine-tunes a pretrained encoder.
Chapter 16 trains a mini-GPT, then uses Gemma with instruction tuning and LoRA, and surveys RLHF, multimodality, RAG and reasoning models.

questions.question: Which pretrained LLM does the contents name for text generation in chapter 16?
questions.explanation: 16.3 lists 'Text generation with the Gemma model' (printed 485). The other models are not named on this contents page.

questions.question: List the components of the Transformer that section 15.3 covers.
questions.answer: Dot-product attention, the encoder block, the decoder block, seq2seq with a Transformer, and positional embeddings.

questions.question: Why might the book present sequence-to-sequence learning with RNNs before the Transformer?
questions.answer: So the reader sees the limitations of the recurrent approach and understands what attention-based Transformers improve.

questions.question: What does LoRA stand for, and in which section is it covered?
Which of RLHF, multimodal LLMs, RAG and reasoning models could you explain today? Note the PDF page of the ones you can't.
questions.answer: RLHF p.519, multimodal LLMs p.522, RAG p.525, reasoning models p.526.
